articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass We have all experienced this: you open your phone because you're bored, scroll through social media for a few mi…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built We have all experienced this: you open your phone because you're bored, scroll through social media for a few minutes, and suddenly an hour has disappeared. What if your phone could give you a reason to put it down? That's why I built GrassTime 🌱 — an app designed to help people break the cycle of mindless scrolling by giving them fun, AI-generated, real-world challenges. Instead of endlessly scrolling when you're bored, open GrassTime and get a challenge to try in the real world! Here's what you can do: 🌿 Discover random challenges: Get fun activities that encourage you to step away from your screen. 🤖 AI-generated ideas: Challenges are generated using Qwen, an open-weight AI model.
articles.author: Harsh Mahajan

articles.title: I built a free tool that shows where your system design breaks — with maths, not servers
articles.excerpt: Whiteboard designs never push back. You draw a load balancer, two servers and a database, someone asks "what happens at 5,000 requests per second?", and nobody really knows. So I built System Canvas:…
articles.body: Whiteboard designs never push back. You draw a load balancer, two servers and a database, someone asks "what happens at 5,000 requests per second?" , and nobody really knows. So I built System Canvas : a free, browser-based canvas where you design an architecture and simulate traffic through it. A design with a CDN, a load balancer, two servers in a VPC, Redis, a SQL database and a payment-service microservice. You can keep it to a single design, like one service with its load balancer, servers and database. Or you can model a microservice system: design each service on its own canvas, connect the services at the top level, and simulate the whole system or benchmark one service at a time. Each microservice gets its own canvas, listed under Services. Components are grouped by category.

articles.title: Exposing Email Cron Errors and Adding Real‑Time Observability to the VS API
articles.excerpt: Exposing Email Cron Errors and Adding Real‑Time Observability to the VS API TL;DR: I refactored the email cron to stop swallowing SMTP/Brevo failures and to surface them through our observability laye…
articles.body: Exposing Email Cron Errors and Adding Real‑Time Observability to the VS API TL;DR: I refactored the email cron to stop swallowing SMTP/Brevo failures and to surface them through our observability layer. The change adds a scoped error reporter, propagates failures to the cron‑trigger controller, and ships a new test suite that guarantees errors aren’t hidden again. The Problem Our nightly runEmailCron() job ( apps/api/src/email/email.cron.ts ) was designed to send a batch of reminder emails. When the underlying SMTP provider (Brevo) rejected a message, the sendMail() helper caught the exception and silently marked the notification as sent .

articles.title: Recruiting Candidate Search Retrieval — Freshness, Access, and Citation Gate
articles.excerpt: Short answer: for recruiting candidate search, use vector retrieval for durable candidate profiles, web retrieval for live role and availability context, and keep the two behind one retrieval contract…
articles.body: Short answer: for recruiting candidate search, use vector retrieval for durable candidate profiles, web retrieval for live role and availability context, and keep the two behind one retrieval contract that always carries tenant, access, and citation metadata. That decision is less about picking a fashionable database than defining what a grounded answer is allowed to say. A recruiter should be able to open the source behind “three backend candidates who can start next month,” and the system must not leak a profile across tenants. I build the contract first, then swap retrieval backends behind it. What should recruiting candidate search retrieval return? Start with the user-visible answer. A result is not just a chunk of text; it is evidence with a route back to the source.

articles.title: Instagram comment-to-DM automation: the limits you design around
articles.excerpt: "Comment PRICE and I will send you the list" looks like the simplest automation there is. A keyword, a direct message, done. I build DOS AI (dosai.pro), where businesses set up AI assistants for Whats…
articles.body: "Comment PRICE and I will send you the list" looks like the simplest automation there is. A keyword, a direct message, done. I build DOS AI (dosai.pro), where businesses set up AI assistants for WhatsApp, Instagram and Telegram, and this feature ended up shaped almost entirely by what Instagram will not let you do. Here are the limits and what we built around each. You cannot write first, and a comment is the exception A business cannot start a conversation in Instagram. Not by hand through a tool, not with a bot. The person starts it, with a direct message or with a comment. So a comment is more valuable than it looks: it is permission to send one private reply. One. After that single message you are silent until the person answers.
articles.author: DOS AI

articles.title: Appointment reminders in a chat bot: six rules we ended up with
articles.excerpt: I build DOS AI (dosai.pro), a platform where a small business sets up an AI assistant for WhatsApp, Instagram and Telegram. Booking is a core feature there, and the part that sounds trivial, "send a r…
articles.body: I build DOS AI (dosai.pro), a platform where a small business sets up an AI assistant for WhatsApp, Instagram and Telegram. Booking is a core feature there, and the part that sounds trivial, "send a reminder before the visit", turned out to hold most of the rules. None of this is about the model. The reminder texts are templates, not generated, and they cost the owner nothing. The work was deciding when not to send. 1. Night is a hard wall Messages about a booking go out between 9:00 and 21:00 in the project's time zone. Two cases fall out of that: A reminder that would land at night is sent the evening before, at 20:30. A 9:30 visit with a "two hours before" reminder gets it at 20:30 the previous day, not at 7:30. A confirmation for a booking created at night goes out at 9:00.

articles.title: Touch Grass AI: Offline AI That Turns Screen Time into Real-World Missions
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Touch Grass AI is an offline-first application designed to help people step away from their screens and engage w…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Touch Grass AI is an offline-first application designed to help people step away from their screens and engage with the real world. Instead of recommending more content to consume, it generates personalized outdoor missions based on the user's mood, available time, energy level, budget, and surroundings. For example, a user might say: "I'm bored, have 30 minutes, and don't want to spend any money." Touch Grass AI can generate a mission such as Mini Explorer, encouraging the user to explore a safe nearby area, discover different types of leaves, and notice things they usually overlook. The goal is simple: use AI to encourage real-world experiences rather than more screen time.

articles.title: NASA Demonstrates Next-Generation Heat Shield Technologies
articles.excerpt: NASA is testing heat shields that can keep astronauts safe as they return from missions to the Moon and Mars in an unusual way: by taking out the trash. When Northrop Grumman 24th cargo resupply missi…
articles.body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) A KREPE-3 capsule floats inside the Northrup Grumman Cygnus XL 24 cargo spacecraft on October 7. Inside the capsule is a 3-D printed heat shield designed by researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. NASA NASA is testing heat shields that can keep astronauts safe as they return from missions to the Moon and Mars in an unusual way: by taking out the trash. When Northrop Grumman 24 th cargo resupply mission for NASA undocked from the International Space Station, it carried a fleet of 12 small, experimental capsules designed to test the next generation of thermal protection materials that could serve as the foundation for future heat shields.
